rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following is most basic ?
rows.solution:
For an oxide of a transition metal, the character runs from basic through amphoteric to acidic as the oxidation state of the metal rises. At a low oxidation state the metal keeps its electropositive, metallic character and the bonding is ionic, so the oxide is basic; at a high oxidation state the metal pulls electron density strongly towards itself, the bonding turns covalent, and the oxide becomes acidic.

Manganese is \(+2\) in MnO, \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_3}\), \(+4\) in \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) and \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\). The lowest of those is \(+2\), so MnO is the most basic. \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) is at the other end of the range and is acidic, dissolving in water to give permanganic acid.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following solutions will have the highest osmotic pressure ?
rows.solution: Osmotic pressure is a colligative property, \(\Pi = i\,C\,RT\), so with all four solutions at the same concentration and temperature the one with the largest van't Hoff factor exerts the greatest pressure. Glucose and urea are non-electrolytes and do not dissociate, so \(i = 1\) for both. Potassium chloride gives two ions per formula unit, so \(i = 2\). Calcium chloride gives one \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), so \(i = 3\). The \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{CaCl_2}\) solution therefore has the highest osmotic pressure.

rows.stem: For a reaction : \(\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \longrightarrow 2NH_3}\), the rate of reaction with respect to \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is
rows.solution:
Rates of appearance and disappearance are tied to the stoichiometric coefficients, so the single rate of reaction is
\(-\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2}]}{\Delta t} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NH_3}]}{\Delta t}\)

Ammonia has the coefficient 2, so its term is divided by 2, and the sign is positive because ammonia is being formed. The rate of reaction expressed through ammonia is \(+\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NH_3}]}{\Delta t}\).

rows.stem: How many Faradays are required to reduce 1 mol of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) in acidic medium ?
rows.solution:
Work out the change in oxidation state, not the formula mass. In the dichromate ion each chromium is \(+6\); in \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) it is \(+3\). So each chromium atom gains three electrons, and the ion contains two of them:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Six electrons per ion means 6 mol of electrons for 1 mol of dichromate, so 6 faradays are required.

rows.stem: Which of the following Grignard Reagent will be used to prepare cyclohexylmethanol when treated with methanal ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the PRODUCT in the stem and options (B), (C) and (D) are all printed as DRAWINGS: a plain hexagon carrying one labelled substituent. Only option (A) is printed as text. Read on my own page at 3x: the hexagons carry no double bonds, so they are cyclohexane rings, and the printed substituent labels are, verbatim, CH2OH (stem), CH2MgBr (B), MgBr (C) and CH2CH2MgBr (D). Those four drawings are therefore NAMED here — cyclohexylmethanol, cyclohexylmethylmagnesium bromide, cyclohexylmagnesium bromide, 2-cyclohexylethylmagnesium bromide — which is a lossless reading and the route this addendum prefers, and it does NOT state the answer: a student must still know that a Grignard plus methanal adds exactly one carbon, which is the whole discrimination the question tests. The real crops should still be attached. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Methanal is the smallest aldehyde and has no carbon substituent of its own, so a Grignard reagent adding to it contributes the whole of the rest of the molecule and the product is a PRIMARY alcohol one carbon longer than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{R-MgBr} + \mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{R-CH_2-OH}\)

Cyclohexylmethanol is cyclohexyl-\(\mathrm{CH_2}\)-OH, so R must be the cyclohexyl group and the reagent is cyclohexylmagnesium bromide. Using the cyclohexylmethyl reagent instead would give one carbon too many, and methylmagnesium bromide would give only ethanol.

rows.stem: The secondary valency of Pt in \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\) is
rows.solution:
The secondary valency is the coordination number, the count of ligand donor atoms bonded directly to the metal. Here the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are BIDENTATE, each donating through two nitrogen atoms, so they supply four donor atoms between them, and the two chlorido ligands supply one each. That makes six donor atoms round the platinum, so the secondary valency is 6.

Counting ligand MOLECULES rather than donor ATOMS gives 4, which is the trap this question is built on.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - OC_2H_5}\) on reaction with HI gives
rows.solution:
Cleavage of an ether by hydrogen iodide gives an alcohol and an alkyl iodide, and which fragment keeps the oxygen depends on the groups. Here one group is tertiary, so after the ether is protonated the reaction takes the unimolecular route: the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond to the tertiary carbon breaks to give the relatively stable tertiary carbocation, which the iodide ion then captures.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-OC_2H_5} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)

So the iodine goes to the tertiary group and the ethyl group keeps the oxygen as ethanol. Had both groups been primary, the mechanism would have been bimolecular and the iodide would have attacked the LESS hindered carbon instead.

rows.stem: An example of non-reducing sugar is
rows.solution:
A sugar is reducing if it still has a free aldehydic or ketonic group able to reduce Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution. Glucose is a monosaccharide and has one. Maltose and lactose are disaccharides whose glycosidic linkage leaves one reducing group free, so both are reducing sugars.

In sucrose the linkage is between C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose — that is, between the reducing group of each unit. Neither is left free, so sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.

rows.stem: Benzene diazonium chloride on reaction with phenol in weakly basic medium gives
rows.solution:
This is azo coupling. In weakly basic medium phenol is converted partly to the phenoxide ion, which is even more strongly activated, and the benzenediazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile attacking the position para to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\):
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-OH\ (p)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product is p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye. Azobenzene itself would need benzene, which is not activated enough to couple; chlorobenzene and benzene are products of quite different diazonium reactions.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The presence of –OH group in phenols directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions.
Reason (R) : –OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution reaction.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group donates its lone pair into the ring by resonance. That does two things at once. It raises the electron density of the ring as a whole, so phenol is far more reactive than benzene towards electrophiles — the Reason, and it is true. And it raises that density specifically at the ortho and para positions, so those are where the electrophile attacks — the Assertion, also true.

Both statements are true, and since it is the same resonance donation that produces both effects, the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show irregularities in their electronic configurations.
Reason (R) : In actinoids 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are of comparable energies.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Actinoids do show irregular electronic configurations, and their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are indeed of comparable energy, so both statements are true.

The Reason explains why actinoids show a WIDE RANGE OF OXIDATION STATES, which is a different consequence. The irregularities in the ground state configurations come from the special stability of half-filled and fully filled subshells, which occasionally makes one arrangement preferable to the one the filling order predicts. So both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Components of azeotropes are easily separated by fractional distillation.
Reason (R) : Components of an azeotrope have same composition in liquid and vapour phase.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The components of an azeotrope cannot be separated by fractional distillation, so the Assertion is false. The Reason states correctly that an azeotrope has the same composition in the liquid and the vapour phase, so it is true.

Indeed the Reason is exactly why the Assertion fails. Fractional distillation works only because ordinary vapour is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it came from; when the two compositions are identical there is nothing for successive vaporisations to enrich, and the mixture distils over unchanged. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The two strands of DNA are complementary to each other.
Reason (R) : The hydrogen bonds are formed between specific pairs of bases.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The two strands of DNA are complementary, so the Assertion is true, and hydrogen bonds do form between specific pairs of bases, so the Reason is true.

The pairing is what complementarity MEANS here: adenine hydrogen bonds only to thymine, through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine only to cytosine, through three. Because each base has exactly one partner, the sequence of one strand fixes the sequence of the other, which is what lets DNA be replicated. The Reason is therefore the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
What type of deviation from Raoult’s law is shown by mixture of ethanol and acetone ? Give reason.
What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing ethanol and acetone ?
rows.solution:
A mixture of ethanol and acetone shows positive deviation from Raoult's law. In pure ethanol the molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonds between one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and the next. Acetone has no hydrogen on oxygen, so an ethanol molecule surrounded by acetone molecules loses most of that hydrogen bonding and gains only a weaker interaction in its place. The molecules are therefore held less tightly after mixing than before, more of them escape into the vapour, and each partial vapour pressure rises above the value Raoult's law predicts.

Since the total vapour pressure of the mixture is raised, it reaches the external pressure at a lower temperature. The boiling point of the solution therefore decreases.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between the following :
(i) Acidic amino acids and basic amino acids
(ii) Nucleotide and Nucleoside
rows.solution:
(i) The classification depends on which functional group is in excess in the side chain. An acidic amino acid is one carrying more \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) groups than \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups, as in aspartic acid and glutamic acid. A basic amino acid is one carrying more \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups than \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) groups, as in lysine and arginine. When the two are equal in number the amino acid is neutral, which most of them are.

(ii) A nucleoside is a nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar, so nucleoside = base + sugar. A nucleotide is that nucleoside further joined to phosphoric acid, so nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate. It is the nucleotide, not the nucleoside, that is the repeating unit of a nucleic acid, because the phosphate group is what links one unit to the next.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Anomers
(b) Invert sugar
(c) Glycosidic linkage
rows.solution:
(a) Anomers are a pair of stereoisomers of a monosaccharide that differ in configuration at one carbon only — the anomeric carbon, C-1 in an aldose and C-2 in a ketose. That carbon becomes a new stereocentre when the open chain closes into its cyclic hemiacetal form. \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose are the standard pair, differing only in whether the C-1 hydroxyl points below or above the ring.

(b) Invert sugar is the equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose obtained by hydrolysing sucrose. The name records a change of SIGN. Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory, but its hydrolysis gives dextrorotatory glucose together with fructose, which is so strongly laevorotatory that it outweighs the glucose. The net rotation of the product mixture is therefore to the left: the rotation has been inverted.

(c) A glycosidic linkage is the oxygen bridge that joins two monosaccharide units, formed when the hydroxyl groups of the two units condense and a molecule of water is lost. It is the linkage that builds disaccharides and polysaccharides — the \(\alpha\)-1,4 bonds of maltose and starch, the \(\beta\)-1,4 bonds of cellulose.
